It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Inverting buck-boost converter calculator work?
sections.html:
The Inverting buck-boost converter takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports input voltage (Viₙ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the output voltage (Vₒuₜ), the maximum ripple current (Iriₚₚₗₑ), the duty cycle (D) and the inductance (L).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Inverting buck-boost converter calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Input voltage (Viₙ)=-output voltage (Vₒuₜ) + output voltage (Vₒuₜ) ÷ duty cycle (D)
Switching frequency (fₛw)=duty cycle (D) × input voltage (Viₙ) ÷ (inductance (L) × maximum ripple current (Iriₚₚₗₑ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Output voltage (Vₒuₜ) = 10 V and Duty cycle (D) = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives Input voltage (Viₙ) = 90 V.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Input voltage (Viₙ) = 90 V should be roughly the size you expected from Output voltage (Vₒuₜ) = 10 V and Duty cycle (D) = 10 %.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in volts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilohertz, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Frequency, opening in kilohertz
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in milliamperes
  • %, opening in percent
  • Inductance – henry, opening in microhenries

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Inverting buck-boost converter earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the output voltage, the maximum ripple current and the duty cycle — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Inverting buck-boost converter calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns input voltage (Viₙ), derived from the output voltage, the maximum ripple current and the duty cycle. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Inverting buck-boost converter calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the output voltage, the maximum ripple current, the duty cycle and the inductance, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter input voltage (Viₙ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Input voltage (Viₙ) opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Input voltage (Viₙ) = 90 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Inverting buck-boost converter calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
